titleEn: Five-Year-Old With a Bee Sting at the Park - Paediatric Anaphylaxis

patient.name: Lily Carter
patient.weightEn: 20 kg (her mother: she was weighed at her check-up last month)
patient.affectEn: limp, drowsy and whimpering; held upright on her mother's lap and slumping against her; face flushed, lips and eyelids visibly swollen; wet cough and audible wheeze
patient.speechEn: drowsy and breathless with a hoarse cry: answers her mother's voice with a word or two ('can't... breathe', 'tummy hurts'); her mother answers the history questions for her and the child adds a few words at most

scene.settingEn: Confederation Park in Burnaby, afternoon (dispatch 1432). Sunny, 24 °C, dry. The patient is on a grassy area beside the playground, about 10 m from a garbage bin where a few bees are still buzzing. A paved path lets the stretcher come to within 15 m of the patient. Other children and parents stand back. One patient. Hospital is 8 minutes away.
hazardsEn: a few bees still buzzing around the garbage bin about 10 m from the patient - keep the crew and the patient clear
other children and parents nearby (standing back)

bystanders.who: mother (holding the child upright on her lap)
bystanders.knowsEn: Her daughter is 5 years old and weighed 20 kg at her check-up last month. She was playing near the garbage bin and was stung once on the left forearm about 15 minutes before you arrived. Within minutes her lips swelled and she broke out in hives; she vomited once about 5 minutes before you arrived, then went floppy and sleepy. Onset sudden, the worst reaction she has ever had; the mother gave her nothing and nothing has helped. Last summer a sting caused a large local swelling only, with no breathing trouble. Mild eczema, no asthma, no medications. No known drug or food allergies; no EpiPen. Lunch at 1230, a popsicle about 1415. No one else was stung. She will ride along in the ambulance.
He carried the child about 10 m away from the garbage bin. He has nothing to add beyond what the mother says.
He flagged you from the path to the grassy area. He knows nothing about the child. He will help, for example keep the paved path clear for the stretcher, if you ask him.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with child-sized non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
epinephrine for IM injection, with syringes and IM needles
salbutamol (nebulizer kit and MDI with spacer)
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline

dispatchEn: 1432 hrs. Code 3 to a playground at Confederation Park in Burnaby. 5-year-old female stung by a bee. Her mother reports the child's lips are swelling and she is struggling to breathe. Hospital is 8 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: the mother says her daughter was stung once on the arm near a garbage bin, has no known bee allergy and no EpiPen, and is now very sleepy; a few bees are still around the bin.
arrivalEn: A parks worker flags you from the path to a grassy area beside the playground. It is a sunny afternoon, 24 °C and dry, and the paved path lets the stretcher come to within 15 m. The father has carried the child about 10 m away from the garbage bin, where a few bees are still buzzing. Other children and parents are standing back. Your partner is right behind you with the kits. One patient.
firstLookEn: A small girl limp and drowsy on her mother's lap, held upright and slumping against her mother. Her lips are visibly swollen and her face is flushed. She has a wet cough and you can hear a wheeze from where you stand. A small amount of vomit is on the grass beside them.

primary.locEn: Responds to voice (AVPU = V): drowsy and whimpering, answering her mother's voice with a word or two ('can't... breathe', 'tummy hurts').
primary.airwayEn: Lips and eyelids swollen, hoarse cry, no stridor. She vomited once and a little vomit is still in her mouth. Airway patent but at risk.
primary.breathingEn: Rate 36, laboured, with retractions and audible wheeze. Wet cough.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 146, weak, regular. Hands cool. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Modified rapid body survey for a medical patient: one sting site on the left forearm with the stinger and venom sac still embedded and local swelling; widespread urticaria (hives) over the chest, back and limbs; no other stings; no trauma. Skin: face flushed, widespread hives, hands cool (skin is given automatically during the RBS). C-spine not indicated: a medical call, she sat down on the grass with no fall and no head strike.
primary.skinEn: face flushed, widespread urticaria (hives) over chest, back and limbs, hands cool

history.ccEn: Child (a word or two): "Can't... breathe. Tummy hurts." Mother: "A bee stung her on the arm and her lips swelled up. Now she's struggling to breathe and she's so sleepy."

opqrst.oEn: Mother: "It was all at once. She was playing by the garbage bin and a bee stung her once on the left forearm. Within minutes her lips swelled and she broke out in hives."
opqrst.pEn: Mother: "Nothing has helped. I didn't give her anything."
opqrst.qEn: Child: "Tummy... hurts." Mother: "She says it's hard to breathe. She hasn't said anything else about how it feels."
opqrst.rEn: Mother: "The sting is on her left forearm. The hives are all over her chest, back, arms and legs, and her lips and eyelids are swollen."
opqrst.sEn: Mother: "It's the worst reaction she's ever had."
opqrst.tEn: Mother: "She was stung about 15 minutes before you got here. Her lips swelled within minutes, she threw up once about 5 minutes before you arrived, and then she went floppy and sleepy."

history.painScoreEn: Shown the faces scale for the bee sting on her arm, the child points to 2 out of 10.

sample.sEn: Mother: "Her lips and eyelids are swollen, she's covered in hives, she's wheezy and coughing, she threw up once, and her tummy hurts. Now she's very sleepy." Child: "Can't... breathe."
sample.aEn: Mother: "No allergies that we know of - no drugs, no foods. She's never had an EpiPen. Last summer a sting gave her a big local swelling and that was all, no trouble with her breathing."
sample.mEn: Mother: "Nothing. She doesn't take any medications. I haven't given her anything for this."
sample.pEn: Mother: "She has mild eczema. No asthma. She's five and she weighed 20 kilos at her check-up last month."
sample.lEn: Mother: "Lunch around 12:30, and a popsicle about a quarter past two."
sample.eEn: Mother: "She was playing near the garbage bin when a bee stung her once on the left forearm, and then it all came on within minutes."

fe.generalEn: Mother: "She was healthy and playing normally until the sting."
fe.cnsEn: Mother: "She's dizzy and sleepy. No headache, no seizure."
fe.respiratoryEn: Mother: "She's got a wheezy cough and a hoarse voice." Child: "My chest feels tight."
fe.cardiovascularEn: Child: "My heart is going fast." Mother: "She's never had any heart problems."
fe.giGuEn: Child: "My tummy hurts." Mother: "She threw up once. No diarrhea."
fe.integumentaryEn: Mother: "She's itchy all over with hives, and she has mild eczema on her elbows."
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Mother: "Her left forearm is sore where the bee stung her. Nothing else hurts."
fe.endocrineEn: Mother: "No, nothing like that. She doesn't have diabetes."
fe.eentEn: Mother: "Her lips and eyelids are swollen and her eyes are itchy." Child: "My throat feels funny."

findings.headNeckEn: Lip and eyelid swelling, hoarse voice, no stridor.
findings.chestLungsEn: Expiratory wheeze in all fields on 6-site auscultation, equal air entry on both sides.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Urticaria on both legs. Circulation, sensation and movement intact.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: LEFT forearm: sting site red and swollen, about 4 cm across; the stinger has already been scraped off (if the candidate has not removed it, it is still embedded); urticaria; circulation, sensation and movement intact. RIGHT arm: urticaria; circulation, sensation and movement intact.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, before epinephrine (required before initiating the protocol); unchanged until epinephrine has had time to work
about 5 minutes after the first epinephrine dose, en route: a PARTIAL response - BP still under 90 and she is still wheezing, so the second epinephrine dose is required now

resp.rawEn: 30, wheeze reduced but present, no stridor

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: the next check about 5 minutes after the second epinephrine dose (and the PCP fluid bolus): improving. The scenario states only BP, pulse, SpO2 and the wheeze; every other value is carried over unchanged from set 2

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan epinephrine (weight-based paediatric dose), child-sized oxygen mask, suction, BVM, salbutamol, early transport
triggers: bring the epinephrine and the paediatric kit
bring the epinephrine and the pediatric kit

expected.actionEn: Recognize from dispatch a likely unstable paediatric anaphylaxis (lip swelling, breathing difficulty, sleepy child) and plan to obtain the child's weight on arrival
Anticipate bees still present at the scene; plan PPE and a safe approach
Assign crew roles before arrival: one member on the patient and the protocol, one on the stretcher and egress (p.55)
triggers: you're on the stretcher and egress

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (bees still near the garbage bin - keep crew and patient clear), environment, nature of illness (allergic reaction to a bee sting), number of patients (1)
triggers: allergic reaction to a bee sting

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection
First look: limp, drowsy child on her mother's lap, swollen lips, flushed face, wet cough and audible wheeze, vomit on the grass
Confirm with the mother that no one else was stung
Assess LOC / AVPU: responds to Verbal, drowsy - a decreased LOC finding
Verbalize c-spine not indicated (medical, no fall, no head strike)
Assess airway - swollen lips and eyelids, hoarse cry, vomit in the mouth; clear it and keep suction ready (paediatric suction 10 seconds at most, p.45)
Assess breathing - rate, effort, retractions, wheeze
Assess circulation - fast, weak radial pulse; cool hands
triggers: rate and strength of the pulse

expected.actionEn: Perform a modified rapid body survey: find the sting site and the embedded stinger, look for hives and other stings, rule out trauma
Note skin: flushed, urticaria, cool hands
High-flow oxygen 15 L/min by child-sized non-rebreather mask to keep SpO2 at or above 94% (shortness of breath and shock need high flow, p.50)
Lay the child SUPINE (not held upright on her mother's lap) and do NOT walk her (per the Anaphylaxis protocol, p.55)
Categorize as RTC and act with urgency
Epinephrine given on scene, then ready to load within 15 minutes - no full secondary survey on scene
triggers: give the epi here then transport

expected.actionEn: Delegate the partner to prepare the stretcher and egress (explicitly required by the Anaphylaxis protocol, p.55)
triggers: bring the stretcher up the path

expected.actionEn: Manage the parent: explain what is happening, keep the mother with the child, arrange for her to ride along, and keep the child supine for the carry to the stretcher
Establish chief complaint: swollen lips and difficulty breathing after a bee sting
HxC/C with OPQRRRST/LOTARP: time of the sting, number of stings, time to the first signs, progression (lips, hives, vomiting, drowsiness), reaction to previous stings
triggers: how many times was she stung
how quickly did the swelling start

expected.actionEn: Pain score at the sting site using a faces scale
PMHx (mild eczema, no asthma)
Medications, and whether anything was given for this reaction
Allergies (none known; previous large local reaction to a sting; no EpiPen)
LOI (lunch and a popsicle)
Use the mother as the history source and get the child's weight (20 kg) before any drug dose is calculated
GCS with components, adapted for a child (13: E3 V4 M6)
BP by auscultation with a child-sized cuff - recognize systolic under 90 as an anaphylaxis instability criterion (p.55)
Pulse rate/strength/rhythm
Respirations rate/depth/work of breathing incl wheeze and retractions
triggers: rate depth and work of breathing

expected.actionEn: Skin hands-on: temperature, colour, condition, extent of urticaria
Pupils
SpO2 with calibration
BGL - reasonable with decreased LOC in a child (temperature is not indicated)
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory (pertinent)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (vomiting and abdominal pain are anaphylaxis signs, p.55)
FE - Integumentary (urticaria)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (angioedema)
Head/neck exam incl airway swelling reassessment
triggers: look at the lips and eyelids

expected.actionEn: Chest exam with 6-site auscultation, bilateral comparison
Abdomen exam
Back exam
triggers: run my hands down her back

expected.actionEn: Lower extremities
Upper extremities: sting site, confirm the stinger is removed, CSM

Initiate the Anaphylaxis protocol with the correct indications (signs + bee-sting exposure + instability: systolic under 90, respiratory distress, decreased LOC) and with the baseline vitals done first (p.55)
Remove the allergen: scrape off the embedded stinger (p.55)
State the weight (20 kg) and calculate the epinephrine dose: 0.01 mg/kg x 20 kg = 0.2 mg IM, maximum 0.5 mg - never the 0.5 mg adult dose (p.66)
Administer epinephrine 0.2 mg IM with the 6 rights, correct site (anterolateral thigh) and IM needle; note the time
Keep the child supine and do not walk her or carry her upright to the stretcher (p.55)
Give epinephrine first: treat bronchospasm with salbutamol only AFTER epinephrine, and never use salbutamol or an antihistamine instead of it (p.55)

PCP: after epinephrine give salbutamol at the weight-based dose (nebulized 5 mg, or MDI 5 x 100 mcg for the 10-20 kg band - 20 kg is not over 20 kg) and diphenhydramine (p.64: 25-50 mg, no paediatric dose printed - the lowest listed dose, 25 mg IV)
Verbalize repeat dosing: epinephrine 0.2 mg IM may be repeated up to 3 times if she is still unstable at the 5-6 minute reassessment
triggers: may repeat up to three times
reassess in five minutes and repeat

expected.actionEn: Verbalize withholding Entonox (altered LOC, inability to comply, shock caution - p.65) and oral acetaminophen/ibuprofen (vomiting, drowsy); the mild sting-site pain does not delay epinephrine
Reassess ABCs, the airway swelling and all interventions 5 minutes after epinephrine and after each move (including loading the stretcher)
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes and interpret it as a partial response (BP still under 90, wheeze persists)
Repeat epinephrine 0.2 mg IM (same weight-based dose) when the second set shows she is still hypotensive and wheezing; up to 3 repeats are allowed (p.66)
PCP: vascular access and a 20 mL/kg (400 mL) fluid bolus because she remains hypotensive, reassessed when the bolus is in (p.55)
En-route notification for a critical paediatric patient (airway swelling, hypotension, 20 kg)
Complete hand-off: age, weight, allergen exposure and timeline, baseline and repeat vitals, response to treatment
State each epinephrine dose with its weight-based calculation, time, route and response (0.2 mg IM, twice)
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes (weight and its source, dose calculation, time of each dose and of the fluid bolus)

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate lets the child stand or walk (walks her, or asks her to walk, to the stretcher, along the path or to the ambulance)

candidate deliberately keeps the child sitting up or upright as the plan of care or transport - leaves her sitting on her mother's lap, sits her up, or has her carried upright in someone's arms to the stretcher - after her low blood pressure or distress is known, instead of laying her supine. Holding her briefly to clear vomit or while setting up equipment is NOT this event

candidate actually gives (not merely mentions as the maximum) epinephrine at the 0.5 mg adult dose, or any adult-sized dose not calculated from her weight, to this 20 kg child. A dose stated and corrected before it is given is NOT this event
candidate actually gives epinephrine at a dose other than 0.2 mg (0.01 mg/kg x 20 kg) that is not the adult dose. Record the 0.5 mg adult dose as epi-adult-dose instead
candidate gives epinephrine by a route other than IM (e.g. IV or subcutaneous)
candidate actually gives a second epinephrine dose (the repeat after the first 0.2 mg IM dose). Saying they would repeat it if she stays unstable is NOT this event

candidate actually gives salbutamol at a dose other than the 10-20 kg band dose for this 20 kg child: nebulized other than 5 mg, or MDI other than 5 x 100 mcg (for example 10 x 100 mcg, the over 20 kg dose)
PCP actually gives diphenhydramine at more than 25 mg (for example the full 50 mg adult dose). 25 mg, or a weight-based 1 mg/kg (about 20 mg), is acceptable
PCP runs the fluid bolus past the 20 mL/kg (400 mL) volume, or hangs another bag, without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) once the 400 mL is in

drugs.doseEn: 0.01 mg/kg IM to a maximum of 0.5 mg: 0.2 mg IM for this 20 kg child (NEVER the 0.5 mg adult dose), into the anterolateral thigh with an IM needle, after the baseline vitals; may be repeated up to 3 times - a second 0.2 mg dose is due at the 5-6 minute reassessment when she is still hypotensive and wheezing
drugs.indicationsEn: anaphylaxis: signs + exposure to an allergen + unstable (BP < 90 mmHg, decreased LOC, respiratory distress) - all present here
drugs.contraindicationsEn: no absolute contraindications in life-threatening situations such as anaphylaxis
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

drugs.doseEn: she weighs exactly 20 kg, the 10-20 kg band: nebulized 5 mg, or MDI 5 x 100 mcg per course (NOT the over 20 kg dose of 10 x 100 mcg); may repeat; for bronchospasm ONLY AFTER epinephrine. Contraindication: known hypersensitivity to salbutamol

p.64 lists 25-50 mg IV or PO and no paediatric dose: give the lowest listed dose, 25 mg IV (she is vomiting); a weight-based 1 mg/kg, about 20 mg, is also acceptable textbook practice; ONLY AFTER epinephrine; hypotension is a listed adverse effect, so give it with the bolus running
20 mL/kg IV bolus = 400 mL for 20 kg (maximum 2 L, reassess every 500 mL; a 400 mL bolus is reassessed when it is in), because she remains hypotensive

self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this scenario: altered level of consciousness and inability to comply are contraindications and shock is a caution (p.65); the mild sting-site pain never delays epinephrine. If given, report drug:entonox
oral - WITHHELD in this scenario: she is vomiting and drowsy with a threatened airway (p.58: nausea and vomiting argue against it). If given, report drug:acetaminophen
oral - WITHHELD in this scenario: nothing by mouth for a drowsy, vomiting child with a threatened airway (p.68 pediatric dose is weight-based, 10 mg/kg PO). If given, report drug:ibuprofen

notificationFacts.findings: lip and eyelid angioedema, hoarse voice, no stridor, wheeze in all fields, widespread urticaria, vomiting; partial response after the first epinephrine dose

If rechecked after the second dose: BP 94/58, P 126, SpO2 97% on 15 L, wheeze mild

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: She is limp and drowsy: she responds to voice only, answering her mother with a word or two ('can't... breathe', 'tummy hurts').
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: She is breathing fast and laboured, with retractions and an audible wheeze.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR gives epinephrine 0.2 mg IM (0.01 mg/kg x 20 kg; repeat up to 3 times), scrapes off the stinger, gives high-flow oxygen, keeps the child supine and transports rapidly. Salbutamol is within EMR scope (p.49, p.77) and may follow epinephrine for bronchospasm, although p.55 lists it among the PCP additions; EMR does NOT give diphenhydramine or IV fluids. No Functional Enquiry. Entonox and oral analgesics are withheld (altered LOC, vomiting). Textbook practice (not a BC rubric item): do not squeeze the venom sac when removing the stinger.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access with a 20 mL/kg (400 mL) fluid bolus for persistent hypotension (reassessed when the bolus is in; the 500 mL checkpoint is not reached), salbutamol after epinephrine (nebulized 5 mg, or MDI 5 x 100 mcg for the 10-20 kg band), diphenhydramine (p.64: 25-50 mg and no paediatric dose printed, so the lowest listed dose, 25 mg IV; textbook practice — not a BC rubric item — is a weight-based 1 mg/kg, about 20 mg), and the 9-system Functional Enquiry en route.

sourcePages: Scenario md-13 (data/practical/scenarios-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history (mother), vitals sets 1-2 (set 3 = the scenario's 'next check about 5 minutes later'), FE, exam, interventions, ongoing (partial response: second epinephrine dose required), handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Patients (altered LOC, respiratory distress / accessory muscle use, anaphylaxis; the list is headed Adult, no separate paediatric list); p.13 AVPU (V = responds to verbal, drowsy); p.45 Suctioning (10 seconds in the paediatric patient); p.49 SOB with History of Asthma/COPD (salbutamol within EMR scope); p.50 Oxygen Administration (SOB or shock = high-flow O2, NRB 15 L/min); p.54 Hypovolemia (fluid bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing every 500 mL); p.55 Anaphylaxis (indications: signs + allergen exposure + unstable incl. BP < 90 mmHg; supine and do not walk; scrape off the stinger; SpO2 >= 94%; delegate egress; history and baseline vitals; epinephrine; PCP: vascular access with a 20 mL/kg bolus reassessing every 500 mL, salbutamol after epinephrine, diphenhydramine); p.58 Acetaminophen (nausea / vomiting argue against it); p.64 Diphenhydramine (25-50 mg IV or PO, no paediatric dose printed); p.65 Entonox (contraindications: inability to comply, altered level of consciousness; caution: shock); p.66 Epinephrine (paediatric 0.01 mg/kg IM to a maximum of 0.5 mg, may repeat up to 3 times; no absolute contraindications in anaphylaxis); p.68 Ibuprofen (paediatric 10 mg/kg PO); p.77 Salbutamol (nebulized 5 mg over 1 year; MDI 10-20 kg: 5 x 100 mcg, over 20 kg: 10 x 100 mcg, may repeat up to 3 times).
